correctness.rationale: I reconstructed the all-prime and all-polynomial argument, not just the monomial tests. Euler exponents are (1/n)∑_{d|n} μ(n/d)P(U_d), so their integrality is equivalent to the stated prime-power congruences by Möbius inversion and factoring off each p-part. The ghost sequence tr((M²)^n) has integral Euler exponents by det(I−xM²)^−1; cancelling 8 against odd prime powers in 8U_n²=V_{2n}−2(−1)^n proves sufficiency at odd primes for every even weight. At 2, V_n≡2 mod 4 and doubling give v₂(U_{m2^r})=r for odd m, making r=1 exactly the parity obstruction. Conversely, infinitely many inert odd primes send U_{mp} to −U_m; for each fixed m, integrality forces P(−U_m)=P(U_m) over Z, hence evenness. The equivalent polynomial normal form follows by division by Y−1. For an even weight, clearing denominators in the Binet expansion and pairing conjugates gives the stated rational power. At the root associated with α^{2j₀}, the largest index attaining the maximal positive denominator deficit contributes an odd valuation after clearing; smaller indices cannot hit this root, and larger ones contribute even valuations. With D the stated power of two, extending that valuation gives v(E_P)=odd/D; the ramification index is divisible by D, forcing degree D even over Q(√2)(x), and any rationalizing exponent is divisible by D. Constants and H=0 give rational series. For a nonzero odd part the highest odd exponent contributes an uncancelled irrational log-derivative residue at x=α^{−d}; local Puiseux orders of algebraic functions are rational. The monomial product follows by conjugate pairing; its smallest multipliers follow from the parity test.
